This chapter brings the dissertation to a close by presenting a summary of the key findings of the study, drawing overall conclusions regarding the achievement of the research objectives, and offering recommendations for practice and policy in the context of digital health system adoption in ophthalmology clinics. The chapter concludes by identifying directions for future research and system development arising from the limitations and achievements of the current study.
This dissertation set out to design, develop, and evaluate a web-based

Management System to address the documented inefficiencies of manual and fragmented clinic management practices in ophthalmology settings, with particular reference to the healthcare context of Somalia. The study was guided by five specific research objectives and was framed within four theoretical frameworks: Information Systems Theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, the Diffusion of Innovations framework, and the principles of interoperability and web architecture.
The key findings of the study are as follows. First, the

Management System was successfully designed, implemented, and tested as a full-stack web application comprising twelve functional modules covering patient registration, appointment scheduling, triage, clinical examination, prescription management, pharmacy and inventory management, optical shop management, surgery management, billing and payment processing, multi-branch management, role-based access control, and reporting and analytics. Second, all 88 functional test cases executed across the twelve modules achieved a 100% pass rate, confirming the technical reliability and functional completeness of the system. Third, all

metrics defined for system performance, data accuracy, security enforcement, and usability met or exceeded their defined targets. Fourth, a structured comparative analysis confirmed that the proposed ECMS is the only platform among the five systems reviewed that simultaneously addresses all five research gaps identified in the literature review. Fifth, user acceptance testing confirmed that clinical and administrative staff were able to complete their primary tasks without requiring technical assistance, satisfying the usability requirement defined for the system.

Management System developed in this study represents a purposeful, technically sound, and contextually appropriate digital solution for the operational and clinical management needs of eye care clinics operating in resource-constrained settings. The system successfully eliminates the fragmentation, duplication, and inefficiency associated with paper-based and manual clinic management by providing a centralized, integrated, and role-differentiated digital platform accessible via any standard web browser.

The development and evaluation of the ECMS demonstrates that a full-stack web application delivering comprehensive ophthalmology-specific clinical and administrative functionality can be designed, implemented, and validated within an academic research timeline using widely supported, open-source technologies. The system’s architecture — built on Next.js 15, Node.js, Express.js, PostgreSQL, Prisma ORM, and TypeScript — provides a stable, maintainable, and extensible foundation for future enhancement and clinical deployment.

The study contributes to the body of knowledge in health informatics by providing an empirical demonstration of integrated digital health system design and evaluation in an ophthalmology-specific context, and by addressing a set of research gaps that existing systems in the literature have individually failed to resolve. The findings validate the theoretical frameworks applied in the study and provide evidence that web-based, browser-accessible health information systems represent a viable and appropriate technology pathway for strengthening health information management capacity in resource-limited clinical settings such as those prevalent in Somalia.

It is recommended that eye care clinic administrators in resource-constrained settings consider the adoption of integrated web-based management systems in preference to paper-based or spreadsheet-based approaches. The findings of this study demonstrate that a browser-accessible platform can deliver comprehensive clinical and administrative functionality without requiring specialized client hardware or advanced IT expertise from clinical staff. Clinic management should invest in staff digital literacy training prior to system deployment to maximize adoption rates and minimize resistance to change, consistent with the prescriptions of the Diffusion of Innovations framework.

It is recommended that health policymakers in Somalia and comparable resource-limited settings prioritize the development and adoption of interoperable, web-based health information systems at the clinic level, as a complement to population-level surveillance platforms such as DHIS2. The integration of clinical and administrative management within a single digital platform, as demonstrated by the ECMS, can reduce operational costs, improve data quality, and support evidence-based decision-making at the point of care. Policy frameworks should incentivize the development of locally contextualized digital health solutions rather than the importation of systems designed for high-resource environments.

Development teams building upon or extending the ECMS should prioritize the implementation of a comprehensive audit logging system to support clinical governance and regulatory compliance requirements. Integration with national patient identification systems, where available, should be incorporated to support continuity of care across facilities. Mobile-responsive interface optimization should be considered to extend system accessibility to clinical staff using tablet or smartphone devices in field settings.

7.4.1 Integration of Artificial Intelligence and Decision Support

Future versions of the ECMS could incorporate artificial intelligence and machine learning components to enhance clinical decision support capabilities. Potential applications include automated screening of fundus photographs and anterior segment images for early detection of common ophthalmic conditions such as diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and cataracts; predictive analytics for appointment no-show rates and inventory demand forecasting; and natural language processing for automated extraction of structured clinical data from free-text consultation notes. Such features would build upon the clinical data infrastructure established by the current system and contribute to the evidence base for AI-assisted ophthalmology in resource-limited settings.

The integration of telemedicine capabilities, including secure video consultation between patients and remote ophthalmologists, remote review of clinical examination data and retinal images, and asynchronous store-and-forward referral workflows, represents a high-value extension of the current system. Telemedicine integration would substantially extend the system’s contribution to accessible eye care delivery in under-served areas of Somalia and comparable settings where specialist ophthalmologist availability is severely limited.
